item.title: France deploys 70,000 security personnel as new protests raise riot fears
item.description: Paris has boarded up shops and shut 3 major museums ahead of Saturday's protests, while a football match has been postponed; President Macron acknowledged planning failures after last weekend's unrest ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Samy Adghirni A new round of protests is set to hit France Saturday, raising fears of a repeat of last weekend’s riots. The French government has vowed to subdue any violence, deploying 70.000 security officials, including elite anti-terror forces, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters Friday. He blamed social media calls for violence on the far left.  Shops in Paris including luxury boutiques boarded up windows and hired more security personnel, and some will remain shut. Three popular museums, the Louvre, Musee d’Orsay and the Picasso Museum will close Saturday. The scheduled football match between Paris Saint-Germain and Olympique Lyonnais in Paris was postponed.  “We will be uncompromising with hooligans, looters, and anyone who commits acts of violence — including far-left political groups,” Nunez said, while stressing that the police is “ready” to face rioters. Soldiers will help guard sensitive buildings. Helicopters, water canons and armored vehicles known as Centaurs will also be available. Some cities, including Lyon, banned protests on Saturday and extended curfews.  President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday acknowledged “planning failings and elements of surprise” last weekend, when protests drew more than half a million people and degenerated into vandalism. Rioters attacked public buildings and looted stores across the country. The French leader, who postponed a planned tour across West Africa, blamed ultra-left groups for what he called seditious acts.  Supported by a disparate movement of social media figures, students, unions and left-wing parties, Saturday’s protests are framed as an “Acte II,” or second round, of a movement calling for better public services and government help with the cost of living. Much of the anger is targeted at Macron, who six months before the end of his second term, has never been so unpopular. Polls show the violence has benefited far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner for next year’s election. Adding to tensions, Le Pen is due to convene thousands of supporters in the central city of Orleans on Saturday for her National Rally party congress. Anti-Le Pen opponents are heading there to protest. The unrest has also increased fears about public finances. While France dodged a downgrade at Moody’s Ratings late Friday, it’s struggling to reduce the budget deficit ahead of the 2027 election. A closely watched gauge of bond risk rose to levels last seen during the euro-area debt crisis: The spread between 10-year yields in France and Germany, the region’s safe asset, reached 178 basis points on Thursday, compared with just 85 basis points at the start of September. Private-sector economic activity also shrank this month, with the Composite Purchasing Managers’ Index compiled by S&P Global dropping to 48.4 in October from 51.1 last month. That’s below the 50 threshold separating expansion from contraction. France isn’t the only European country dealing with a popular anger. In Italy, demonstrations by students and other youth are expected in Milan and Rome over the weekend. The government has said will deploy military forces in Milan after protests led to looting and rioting there last weekend.  Protests are also expected in Belgium while Albania is grappling with a second week of violent student-led demonstrations fueled by discontent with Prime Minister Edi Rama’s rule.

item.title: OpenAI resumes training AI, blocks internet access over security risks
item.description: The company said it would keep its most advanced models offline during training until safeguards are adequate, following incidents in which AI systems accessed the web and breached external systems ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Rachel Metz OpenAI has begun cutting off internet access for its most capable artificial intelligence models during the training process in response to prior incidents in which its systems breached other companies. The company said in a blog post Friday that, after a pause last month, it had resumed training its most advanced models but intends to block internet access until it feels it has adequate safeguards in place to mitigate the risk of unreleased models being able to take unapproved actions online during training.  “Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company wrote. In late September, the company said it would pause training its most advanced AI models after it discovered that one of its AI agent systems that was being trained in what was supposed to be a secured, internet-free environment was able to gain access to the web to reach an external, third-party chatbot. At the time, OpenAI described the breakout as the first security incident of its kind since a combination of models gained internet access during internal testing and inadvertently breached the system of the AI platform Hugging Face in July.  The models involved in the inadvertent Hugging Face breach were operating without the usual safety guardrails, the company has said, because OpenAI had intended them to remain in a testing area known as a “sandbox” — essentially, an isolated virtual software environment that’s meant to run security tests or analyse unsafe code in a controlled way. The models were able to break out of that sandbox, however, by leveraging a software vulnerability to access the open internet. OpenAI said that after the Hugging Face incident, it reduced the connections through which its models might be able to reach the internet during training and testing but kept some for the purpose of metrics, logging and authentication. It also spent a vast amount of computing power on tasking agentic AI systems with identifying vulnerabilities in its training environments as part of a red-teaming effort, a phrase typically used to describe deliberate attempts to break into systems to uncover vulnerabilities before real attackers can. “Our red-teaming agents found vulnerabilities in almost every one of these services that gave them limited forms of internet access,” the firm said in its post. The company said it has since deployed software patches, imposed tighter network restrictions and disclosed the findings to vendors. There have been a series of disclosures in recent months from OpenAI and rivals including Anthropic PBC about incidents in which their models carried out self-directed attacks or unsanctioned actions on third-party websites and systems.  These cases, and a series of stark warnings from within the industry, have vaulted the safety debate into the mainstream. AI developers have warned that their systems could soon become too sophisticated for people to control, adding to concerns the technology could be used by malicious human actors to create bioweapons or carry out devastating cyberattacks.

item.title: German firms see India as manufacturing, R&D hub, not just market: Goyal
item.description: German companies are increasingly viewing India as a strategic hub for manufacturing, research and development, and innovation alongside its role as a key consumer market, Commerce and Industry ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Economy / News / German firms see India as manufacturing, R&D hub, not just market: Goyal

German firms see India as manufacturing, R&D hub, not just market: Goyal Piyush Goyal said German companies, including Siemens Healthcare, Volkswagen and Skoda, see India as a partner for manufacturing, research and innovation. Around 2,000 German firms operate in India

Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal | Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India Berlin 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 24 2026 | 1:36 PM IST

Listen to This Article

German companies are increasingly viewing India as a strategic hub for manufacturing, research and development, and innovation alongside its role as a key consumer market, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has said. Addressing the media after concluding his two-day visit here, the minister said he held a series of bilateral meetings with representatives from companies including Siemens Healthcare, Bertelsmann Investment, Volkswagen and Skoda. "The CEOs echoed one message - German companies no longer see India only as a market, but as their partner, as a base for manufacturing, for research and development, for innovation," he said. German precision and research, combined with India's skill and talent to innovate and manufacture for the future, and investing in the India growth story, will change the global perspective and outlook toward India, he said.

About 2,000 German firms currently have operations in India. The minister was here to discuss ways to boost trade and investments between the two countries. Also Read

Govt to bear certification costs for micro, small exporter under EPM: Goyal

India-EU FTA may be operational in January-March, says Piyush Goyal

India-US trade deal would be concluded at the earliest: Sitharaman

First tranche of India-US deal close to conclusion, says Piyush Goyal

US trade pact to be operationalised once India gets competitive edge: Goyal

He added that relations between the two countries open doors not just for trade in goods and services, but also open the door for talent, innovation, co-creating, co-designing, co-developing, and co-manufacturing. "The focus of this visit has been to translate this partnership to greater levels of investment, industrial cooperation, and research and development," he said, adding that the success of the India-EU free trade agreement in the years to come will be measured by new business, new orders, greater investments, and technology partnerships.

The India-European Union trade pact would be signed by the end of this year and may be implemented next year. In January, the two sides concluded negotiations for the agreement. "Today the greatest imperative before German industry is to cut costs and become more competitive in global markets. Therefore, they are looking at manufacturing in a much greater degree in India. As regards their innovation and their design work, almost every company tells me about existing centers, GCCs, in a big way in India, where they employ lakhs of talented young boys and girls," he said. He said, India's over 2,100 global capability centres (GCCs) employ millions of people, with individual centres ranging from a few hundred employees to several lakh. He added that German companies are planning significant expansions, with most aiming to double or triple their operations over the next two to five years.

"That is the level of excitement about working in India... Gradually, this is obviously going to result in co-creation and co-innovation also. But I would like to go step by step. And I'd like to invite the German Institutes of Research and to come there and start working and take the next step forward for developing this partnership," he said. India-EU FTA & CBAM:   Goyal said the European Union appreciates India's efforts to address climate change and its progress in meeting its commitments under the Paris Agreement, including exceeding its intended nationally determined contributions ahead of schedule. He added that European countries want to partner with India in areas such as green hydrogen, financial assistance and its green initiatives.

Referring to his remarks on the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) on Thursday here at the Berlin Global Dialogue, he maintained that what he said a day earlier was completely factual. However, he added that in the current context, Europe was ahead of many other countries on environmental issues and its partnership with India in this area was also progressing rapidly. The minister has said that the EU is inviting "disaster" by imposing CBAM. "Who's responsible for this (climate change) mess in the first place? Where did this ozone layer get damaged? Who sent all that carbon up there?" he asked.

To this, a fellow panellist at the Dialogue said, "All of us". To this, Goyal said: "No, I'm sorry". He added, India supports 17 per cent of the world's population, and the country's contribution in global carbon emission is less than 3 per cent. Goyal, during the talks, mentioned the 2015 Paris Agreement: "It was agreed that the developed countries, who have enjoyed the fruits of messing up the climate for so many decades, will pay a greater price and will support the developing and less developed countries. Eleven years later, we haven't seen a nickel or a dime of that. It's all promises".

He added that European countries caused the problem. "For good reasons... you were growing, you wanted low cost of energy. You blew coal day in and day out so that your energy cost remains low," he said. Goyal emphasised that India has one of the fastest-growing clean energy programmes. Participation in global fairs:   When asked about the commerce ministry's plan to write to Indian Missions abroad about preparing a list of global fairs and exhibitions, Goyal said he would talk to External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar and together "we will reach out to all the missions so that we can create a buzz globally of the India story, the India strength".

Goyal said India is strengthening its presence at major international startup and technology events, with a large delegation expected to attend Finland's Slush programme and a strong Indian pavilion planned at a startup event in France. He cited India's participation in Bharat Innovates 2026 in France and VivaTech, where it had the largest country representation.

item.title: India's Scotch probe of Diageo, Pernod undermines UK pact benefits: ISWAI
item.description: The liquor industry group representing Diageo and Pernod Ricard said that India's move to exclude bulk Scotch imports from the reduced tariff contradicts the trade pact ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / News / India's Scotch probe of Diageo, Pernod undermines UK pact benefits: ISWAI

India's Scotch probe of Diageo, Pernod undermines UK pact benefits: ISWAI The liquor industry group representing Diageo and Pernod Ricard said that India's move to exclude bulk Scotch imports from the reduced tariff contradicts the trade pact

Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the offices of Pernod and Diageo and questioned executives this month as part of an investigation into whether they misclassified imported products (Photo: AdobeStock)

Reuters NEW DELHI 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 24 2026 | 11:11 AM IST

Listen to This Article

India's move to exclude bulk Scotch imports from a reduced 75 per cent tariff goes against provisions agreed in an India-UK trade deal, a group representing liquor makers Diageo and Pernod Ricard wrote in a letter seen by Reuters. Whisky tariffs were a sticking point during the years of protracted negotiations leading up to the deal's July 15 implementation, though India ultimately agreed to halve import taxes on certain Scotch imports from 150 per cent to 75 per cent immediately and to 40 per cent over 10 years. The British government said "iconic UK products" like whiskies would benefit from the pact. Indian investigators, however, have privately told companies the reduced rate does not apply to bulk Scotch concentrates, creating the first significant dispute over the free trade agreement since it took effect.   India's Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the offices of Pernod and Diageo and questioned executives this month as part of an investigation into whether they misclassified imported products to benefit from the reduced rate. Classification issue risks undermining pact, group says In a letter to India's commerce minister on Friday, the International Spirits and Wines Association of India wrote that the classification issue "risks undermining, in practice, an important market-access benefit negotiated and agreed between India and the United Kingdom". Also Read

Tax dept probes Pernod, Diageo Scotch imports under UK trade pact

Pernod Ricard India sales grow 19% in Sep quarter; IPO plan awaits approval

UK trade delegation signs growth partnership with businesses in Maharashtra

India-US trade deal talks nearing 'landing point', says Jaishankar

Govt's free trade push could lead to $140 billion GDP gain for India

"The preferential tariff treatment negotiated ... could effectively become unavailable for these imports," continued the letter, a copy of which was seen by Reuters. ISWAI declined to comment on its letter, while India's commerce ministry did not immediately respond. Pernod, which counts India as its biggest market by volume, declined to comment. Diageo did not respond to a request for comment. Both told Reuters earlier this week that they were cooperating with Indian authorities carrying out the investigation. In the British government's first comment on the controversy, a spokesperson said: "We are working with the government of India to resolve this issue to ensure UK businesses can export under the tariffs agreed in the trade deal." Import tariff disputes have long been a sore point for foreign investors in India, who have in the past faced demands for large amounts of back tax. Such disputes have embroiled the likes of Samsung and Volkswagen. Pernod faces antitrust cases in India and a $314 million back-tax demand from Indian authorities, who accuse it of undervaluing some imports. The company denies wrongdoing. Big implications for India's drinks sector ISWAI's letter underscores the shockwaves the investigation has sent through India's $65 billion alcohol market. Britain accounts for almost 75 per cent of India's imported spirits, primarily driven by Scotch whisky, according to Crisil Ratings. Indian government inspectors have told companies that they do not benefit from the reduced 75 per cent tariff on bulk imports of Scotch concentrates, which must be declared under a customs classification that attracts a 150 per cent duty, three people with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters. Pernod and Diageo import bulk concentrates, mixing them with other ingredients to produce hugely popular Indian brands like Royal Stag, Blenders Pride and McDowell's. The three people said companies including Diageo and Pernod believe concentrates imported from Britain should benefit from the new, lower tariff. ISWAI said in its letter that the India-UK agreement expressly provides preferential tariff treatment for whisky under the relevant tariff lines. An urgent clarification could ensure market-access benefits negotiated by India and Britain are realised "while avoiding uncertainty and disruption for legitimate industry participants", the letter said. On Saturday, the UK-based Scotch Whisky Association told Reuters in a statement that the import of bulk Scotch is key to whisky's overall success in India and that upholding the core principles of the bilateral pact is vital. The association, which counts Diageo and Pernod's Chivas Brothers as members, added the industry was "committed to working in partnership with the UK and Indian governments on the smooth implementation of the deal", so its benefits are unlocked.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
